Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 27, verses 10–11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the messengers fear not in My presence, except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil.﴾

So, on the reading where there is no connection (of the exception to what precedes it), the fear is negated from the messengers and affirmed for whoever has wronged and then repented. On the reading where it is connected, the meaning is: nor anyone else, except the one who has wronged.

As for the saying of some people, that (illa, "except") means (wa, "and"), so that the meaning is "nor the one who has wronged," this is confusion on their part. This would remove security from the language and create ambiguity in the discourse. (Wa, "and," and illa, "except," are mutually contradictory: one of them establishes for the second term a ruling similar to the first, while the other negates that ruling for the second.)

So the claim that the two are interchangeable is baseless, both linguistically and by common usage. The principle is that particles do not substitute for one another, lest ambiguity arise and the meaning intended by the particle be lost. Rather, a verb is given the sense of another verb that requires that particle, so that mentioning one verb together with the particle that another verb requires stands in place of mentioning both verbs. This is one of the marvels and perfections of the language.

Even if we grant that particles interchange and substitute for one another, that happens only when the meaning is clear and ambiguity is safe, and it falls under the category of variety and expansiveness in discourse.

But to claim this without a verbal indicator in the wording is not valid.

We will discuss this at length in a separate section, God willing.

What led them to claim this is that, seeing that fear was negated for what comes after (illa), they thought it meant (wa, "and"), since the meaning seems to require that. But they erred in this, for fear is established for him in the state of his wrongdoing and in the state of his substituting good for evil.

As for the state of his wrongdoing, this is evident. As for the state of substitution, it is because he fears that he has not fulfilled the obligation and that what he did has not been accepted from him.

As in al-Tirmidhi, from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said:

"I said: O Messenger of Allah, ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ — is it the man who commits adultery, steals, and yet fears?

He said: O daughter of Abu Bakr (al-Siddiq), it is the man who fasts, prays, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."

So whoever has wronged and then repented is more deserving of fear, even if no fear were upon him. The disconnection (of the exception) may also occur in this istithna' from another aspect: what follows illa is an independent sentence in itself, so it is disconnected from what precedes it, the way sentences are disconnected from one another. It is called disconnected (munqati') on this basis, as its counterpart was mentioned earlier. And God knows best.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 27, verses 15–16:

As for His saying, ﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾, it refers to the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, and nothing else.

This is the agreed view of the scholars of tafsir (exegesis) and others. The reason is that David, peace be upon him, had many children besides Solomon. If the inheritance had been wealth, Solomon would not have been singled out for it.

Furthermore, the speech of Allah is too exalted to report something of this kind, for it would be like saying: "So-and-so died and his son inherited from him." It is known that every person is inherited from by his son, and there is no benefit in reporting such a thing. Also, what comes before and after the verse shows that the intended inheritance is the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, not the inheritance of wealth. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave David and Solomon knowledge, and they said: "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us above many of His believing servants." And Solomon inherited from David﴾.

This was only mentioned to show the excellence of Solomon and the honour Allah bestowed upon him, and that what he inherited from his father was among the highest gifts, namely knowledge and prophethood. ﴿Indeed, this is surely a manifest favour.﴾

Similarly, the words of Zakariyya, peace be upon him: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You].﴾

This is the inheritance of knowledge, prophethood and the call to Allah. Otherwise, one should not think of a noble prophet that he feared his kinsmen would inherit his wealth, so that he would ask Almighty Allah for a son to prevent them from inheriting it and be more entitled to it than they. Allah has declared His prophets and messengers free of this and similar things. Woe, then, to the one who distorts the Book of Allah, rejects His Messenger's words, and attributes to the prophets what they are innocent of and exalted above. Praise be to Allah for His guidance and success.

[Section: Mention of the speech of the ant]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his hosts of jinn and men and birds, and they were marshalled in ranks...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech.﴾

Allah, glory be to Him, informs us about the ant that He has placed in it the like of this awareness and speech, especially this particular ant, which combined in this address calling, specification, identification, warning, command, the attribution of dwellings to their owners, the seeking of refuge by them in their dwellings so that no other animals enter their dwellings, warning, and apology, all in the most concise address and the sweetest of words. For this reason, Solomon, peace be upon him, took her amazement at her speech as a smile, and it is more fitting for this ant and her kind among the ants to be more knowledgeable of Allah than the Jahmiyyah.

This is indicated by what al-Tabarani narrated in his Mu'jam, he said: al-Dabari related to us from Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from al-Zuhri that Solomon, peace be upon him, went out with his companions seeking rain, and he saw an ant standing and raising one of its legs, asking for rain. So he said to his companions: "Return, for you have been given water; this ant has asked and it has been answered." Imam Ahmad said: Waki' related to us, he said: Mis'ar related to us from Zayd al-Ammi from Abu al-Siddiq al-Naji, he said: Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, went out seeking rain for the people, and he passed by an ant lying on its back, raising its legs toward the sky, and it was saying: "O Allah, we are a creation from Your creation; we have no independence from Your provision. So either You give us water or You destroy us." Solomon, peace be upon him, said to the people: "Return, for you have been watered by the supplication of others than you."

al-Tahawi and al-Tabarani also narrated it from the hadith of Abu al-Siddiq al-Naji, he said: Solomon, peace be upon him, went out seeking rain, and he passed by an ant lying on its back, raising its legs toward the sky, and it was saying: "O Allah, we are a creation from Your creation; we have no independence from Your watering and Your provision. O Allah, so either You water us or You destroy us." He said: "Return, for you have been watered by the supplication of others than you." This is the wording of al-Tabarani's narration. The wording of al-Tahawi is: "Then he came upon an ant standing on its leg, raising its hands, saying: 'O Allah, we are a creation from Your creation; there is no independence for us from Your provision, so do not destroy us for the sins of the children of Adam.' So Solomon said to his companions: 'Return, for you have been watered (by the supplication of others than you).'"

So he said to his companions: Return, for you have been watered.'"

When thirst overcame them, they raised their heads to the sky and cried out to Allah, the Exalted, with one voice. So Allah sent down rain upon them from the sky until they drank and departed. Shaykh al-Islam al-Harawi mentioned, with his chain of narration from Abd Allah ibn Wahb, who said: "Honour the cows, for they have not raised their heads to the sky since the calf was worshipped, out of shame before Allah, Mighty and Majestic." It has also been narrated as a marfu' report from Ibn Wahb, from Yahya ibn Ayyub, from Abu Hind, from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Honour the cows, for they are the chief of the beasts; they have not raised their gaze to the sky out of shame before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since the calf was worshipped.'" The point is that this is the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created people and other living beings, even the dullest of animals, whose dullness is proverbial, namely the cow.

[Section]

Now, the ant is among the most guided of animals, and its guidance is one of the most wondrous things. The little ant leaves its home and seeks its food, even if the way is far for it. When it finds it, it carries it and drives it along winding, distant paths with ascents and descents, in extreme roughness, until it reaches its homes, and stores its provisions in them at the time when that is possible.

When it has stored them, it turns to whatever sprouts from them and splits it into two halves so that it will not germinate. If it sprouts even after being split in two, it splits it into four. When it is afflicted by moisture and fears spoilage and decay, it waits for a sunny day, goes out with it, spreads it at the entrances of its homes, and then returns it inside. No ant eats from what another has gathered. And the guidance of the ant is sufficiently shown by what Allah, glory be to Him, related in the Qur'an about the ant whose speech and address to her companions Solomon heard, when she said: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive.﴾

She began her address with the call that the one addressed hears, then used the indefinite noun, then followed it with the generic noun to indicate generality; then she commanded them to enter their dwellings so that they would be protected from the army; then she informed of the reason for this entering, which is fear that the harm of the army will befall them and Solomon and his hosts will crush them; then she excused the Prophet of Allah and his hosts by saying that they do not perceive it. This is among the most wondrous guidance.

Consider how Allah magnified the matter of the ants by His saying: ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his hosts of jinn and men and birds, and they were marshalled in ranks.﴾ Then He said: ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants...﴾ He informed that they all passed by that valley, and this indicates that the valley was known as the valley of the ants, like the valley of the beasts and the like. Then He informed of what shows the great intelligence of this ant and the precision of her knowledge, in that she commanded them to enter their dwellings specific to them, for she and the ants knew that each group has a dwelling that no one else enters. Then she said: ﴿Lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾, so she combined his name and his description, thereby identifying him by both, and she knew his hosts and their commander. Then she said: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, as if she combined apology for the army's harm by saying they do not perceive, with reproach to the ant nation for not taking their precaution and entering their dwellings. For this reason the Prophet of Allah smiled, laughing at her words, and it is indeed a matter for wonder and smiling.

Al-Zuhri narrated from Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "forbade killing the ant, the bee, the hoopoe, and the shrike." And in the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "A prophet from among the prophets alighted under a tree, and an ant bit him, so he ordered his baggage to be removed, and he ordered the ant colony to be burned. Then Allah revealed to him: 'Because an ant bit you, you have burned a nation of the nations that glorify Allah? Would that it had been one ant.'"

Hisham ibn Hassan mentioned that the people of al-Ahnaf ibn Qays suffered severely from ants, so al-Ahnaf ordered a chair to be placed beside the ovens, sat upon it, recited the tashahhud, then said: "You will surely desist, or I will burn you, and we will do such and such." He said: "So they departed."

Awf ibn Abi Jamilah narrated from Qasamah ibn Zuhayr, who said: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "Every thing has a lord; even the ant has a lord."

Among the wonders of its guidance is that it knows its Lord is above His heavens, upon His throne, as Imam Ahmad narrated in Kitab al-Zuhd from a hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet: "A prophet of the prophets went out with the people seeking rain, and an ant raising its legs to the sky, supplicating while lying on its back, distressed them. So he said: 'Return, for you have been sufficed, or you have been watered by others.'" This report has several chains, and al-Tahawi narrated it in al-Tahdhib and others. Imam Ahmad said: "Solomon ibn Dawud went out seeking rain, and he saw an ant lying on its back, raising its legs to the sky, saying: 'O Allah, we are a creation from Your creation, we have no independence from Your watering and Your provision; so either You water us and provide for us, or You destroy us.' So he said: 'Return, for you have been watered by the supplication of others.'"

And I was told that an ant came out of its home and encountered the half of a locust. It tried to carry it but could not manage, so it went and came back with helpers to carry it together with it. It lifted it from the ground, circled its place, and did not find it, so they departed and left it. It said: "Then it put it down, and returned trying to carry it, but could not. So it went and came with them, lifted it, circled, and did not find it, so they departed." It said: "It did this several times. Then, on the last occasion, the ants formed a circle, placed it in the middle, and cut it apart limb by limb." Our shaykh said: "When I related this story to him, he said: 'Allah, the Exalted, created this ant with a natural abhorrence of lying and an awareness of the punishment of liars.'" The ant is among the most greedy of animals, and its greed is proverbial. It is mentioned that when Solomon, peace be upon him, saw the ant's eagerness and great storing of food, he summoned an ant and asked her: "How much does an ant eat in food each year?" She said: "Three grains of wheat." So he ordered her to be placed in a flask, its mouth sealed, and three grains of wheat placed with her, and he left her for a year as she had said. Then, at the end of the year, he ordered the flask opened and found one and a half grains. He said: "Where is your claim? You claimed your provision each year is three grains." She said: "Yes, but when I saw you busy with the affairs of your own kind, I reckoned the remainder of my life and found it more than the specified period, so I limited myself to half the provision and reserved the other half for myself." Solomon wondered at her great greed, and this is among the most wondrous guidance and gift. Among her greed is that she toils throughout the summer and gathers for winter, knowing that demand is scarce in winter and earning is difficult then, though she is weak yet very strong: she carries many times her own weight and drags it to her home.

Among the wonders of her condition: if you take a dried coriander seed and bring it near your nose, you will smell no scent from it. But when you place it on the ground, an ant comes to it from a distant place. If it cannot carry it, it goes and brings with it a line of ants to carry it. How did she perceive its scent from within her home so quickly and come to it? She perceives by smell from afar what others perceive by sight or hearing. She comes from a distant place to a spot where a person has eaten and some crumbs of bread or other remain, and she carries them off. If the item is larger than her, and she cannot carry it, she goes to her hole and brings with her a group of her companions, and they come like a black thread, one following another, until they help one another to lift and transport it. She comes to an ear of grain and smells it; if she finds it wheat, she cuts and tears it and carries it, but if she finds it barley, she does not. She has keen smell, lofty aspiration, great greed, and boldness in trying to move what is many times her weight. The ants have no leader or chief to direct them, as the bees have, except that they have a scout who seeks sustenance. When he finds it, he informs his companions, and they go out gathered together, each ant striving for the good of the group, not secretly taking any grain for herself apart from her companions.

Among the wonders of their condition: when a man wishes to protect himself from ants, so they do not fall into honey or the like, he digs a pit and places water around it, or takes a large vessel, fills it with water, and puts the thing in it. Then the ant that circles it cannot reach it; it climbs the wall and walks on the ceiling until it comes opposite the thing, and then throws itself upon it. We have tested this ourselves. Once a craftsman heated an iron ring in fire and threw it on the ground to cool, and it happened that an ant was enclosed in the ring. It moved in all directions to get out, but the heat of the fire overtook it, so it kept to the center and middle of the ring, which was its place, the farthest point from the rim.

[Section]

Then consider this weak ant and the cleverness Allah gave her in gathering food, storing it, preserving it, and warding off harm from it. You will see in that lessons and signs. You see that when a group of ants wants to secure food, they leave their trails seeking it. When they find it, they take a path from their trails to it and begin carrying it. You see two companies: one carrying what it has taken to their homes, going along, and another coming out of their homes toward it, not mixing with the first on the way, but like two threads, like a group of people going on a road and another group returning on the other side. When an item becomes too heavy for one, a group of ants gathers around it and helps carry it, like a log or stone that a group of people helps lift. If the one who found it is alone, her companions in the procession help her with it to her home and leave her and it. If the one who came upon it is a group, they help one another with it, then divide it at the door of the home.

Some knowledgeable people reported that he saw from them a wondrous thing one day. He said: "I saw an ant come to the half of a locust and try to lift it from the ground, but could not, so she went a short distance and came back with a group of ants. He said: 'So they lifted that half from the ground. When the ant with her company reached its place, they circled around it and searched, but found nothing, so they returned and put it down. Then she came back, found it, tried to lift it, could not, so she went a short distance and came back with them, lifted it, circled the place, and found nothing; so she went and put it down, then came back and brought them again, lifted it, and circled the place. When they found nothing, they formed a circle, placed that ant in the middle, then pressed upon her and cut her limb by limb, while I was watching.'"

Among the wonders of her intelligence is that when she carries grain to her homes, she breaks it, lest it sprout. If it is of the kind that the two halves sprout, she breaks it into four. When it is touched by dew and moisture and she fears decay, she brings it out to the sun and then returns it to her homes. This is why you sometimes see much grain at the doors of her homes, broken, and then soon after you do not see a single one of it.

And among her intelligence is that she does not make her settlement except on elevated ground, lest the flood overflow onto it and drown it. So you will never see an ant colony in the bottom of a valley, but at its top and above what the flood reaches.

Her intelligence is sufficiently shown by what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, stated in His Book about her words to the ant host when they saw Solomon, peace be upon him, and his hosts: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings; let not Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive.﴾

She spoke with ten kinds of address in this advice: calling, alerting, naming, commanding, stating, warning, specifying, informing, generalizing, and apologizing. Her counsel, with its brevity, included these ten types, and for this reason Solomon was amazed by her words, smiled laughing at them, and asked Allah to grant him the ability to thank Him for His blessing upon him when he heard her speech.

Do not consider such intelligence unlikely from a nation that glorifies its Lord, as is in the Sahih from the Prophet, who said:

A prophet of the prophets descended beneath a tree, and an ant bit him. So he ordered his belongings to be removed from under it, then he burned the ant colony. Then Allah revealed to him: "Because one ant bit you, you burned a nation of nations that glorify Me? Why not just one ant?"

When it is afflicted by moisture and fears spoilage and decay, it waits for a sunny day, goes out with it, spreads it at the entrances of its homes, and then returns it inside. No ant eats from what another has gathered. And the guidance of the ant is sufficiently shown by what Allah, glory be to Him, related in the Qur'an about the ant whose speech and address to her companions Solomon heard, when she said: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive.﴾

She began her address with the call that the one addressed hears, then used the indefinite noun, then followed it with the generic noun to indicate generality; then she commanded them to enter their dwellings so that they would be protected from the army; then she informed of the reason for this entering, which is fear that the harm of the army will befall them and Solomon and his hosts will crush them; then she excused the Prophet of Allah and his hosts by saying that they do not perceive it. This is among the most wondrous guidance.

Consider how Allah magnified the matter of the ants by His saying: ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his hosts of jinn and men and birds, and they were marshalled in ranks.﴾ Then He said: ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants...﴾ He informed that they all passed by that valley, and this indicates that the valley was known as the valley of the ants, like the valley of the beasts and the like. Then He informed of what shows the great intelligence of this ant and the precision of her knowledge, in that she commanded them to enter their dwellings specific to them, for she and the ants knew that each group has a dwelling that no one else enters. Then she said: ﴿Lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾, so she combined his name and his description, thereby identifying him by both, and she knew his hosts and their commander. Then she said: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, as if she combined apology for the army's harm by saying they do not perceive, with reproach to the ant nation for not taking their precaution and entering their dwellings. For this reason the Prophet of Allah smiled, laughing at her words, and it is indeed a matter for wonder and smiling.

Al-Zuhri narrated from Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "forbade killing the ant, the bee, the hoopoe, and the shrike." And in the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "A prophet from among the prophets alighted under a tree, and an ant bit him, so he ordered his baggage to be removed, and he ordered the ant colony to be burned. Then Allah revealed to him: 'Because an ant bit you, you have burned a nation of the nations that glorify Allah? Would that it had been one ant.'"

Hisham ibn Hassan mentioned that the people of al-Ahnaf ibn Qays suffered severely from ants, so al-Ahnaf ordered a chair to be placed beside the ovens, sat upon it, recited the tashahhud, then said: "You will surely desist, or I will burn you, and we will do such and such." He said: "So they departed."

Awf ibn Abi Jamilah narrated from Qasamah ibn Zuhayr, who said: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "Every thing has a lord; even the ant has a lord."

Among the wonders of its guidance is that it knows its Lord is above His heavens, upon His throne, as Imam Ahmad narrated in Kitab al-Zuhd from a hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet: "A prophet of the prophets went out with the people seeking rain, and an ant raising its legs to the sky, supplicating while lying on its back, distressed them. So he said: 'Return, for you have been sufficed, or you have been watered by others.'" This report has several chains, and al-Tahawi narrated it in al-Tahdhib and others. Imam Ahmad said: "Solomon ibn Dawud went out seeking rain, and he saw an ant lying on its back, raising its legs to the sky, saying: 'O Allah, we are a creation from Your creation, we have no independence from Your watering and Your provision; so either You water us and provide for us, or You destroy us.' So he said: 'Return, for you have been watered by the supplication of others.'"

And I was told that an ant came out of its home and encountered the half of a locust. It tried to carry it but could not manage, so it went and came back with helpers to carry it together with it. It lifted it from the ground, circled its place, and did not find it, so they departed and left it. It said: "Then it put it down, and returned trying to carry it, but could not. So it went and came with them, lifted it, circled, and did not find it, so they departed." It said: "It did this several times. Then, on the last occasion, the ants formed a circle, placed it in the middle, and cut it apart limb by limb." Our shaykh said: "When I related this story to him, he said: 'Allah, the Exalted, created this ant with a natural abhorrence of lying and an awareness of the punishment of liars.'" The ant is among the most greedy of animals, and its greed is proverbial. It is mentioned that when Solomon, peace be upon him, saw the ant's eagerness and great storing of food, he summoned an ant and asked her: "How much does an ant eat in food each year?" She said: "Three grains of wheat." So he ordered her to be placed in a flask, its mouth sealed, and three grains of wheat placed with her, and he left her for a year as she had said. Then, at the end of the year, he ordered the flask opened and found one and a half grains. He said: "Where is your claim? You claimed your provision each year is three grains." She said: "Yes, but when I saw you busy with the affairs of your own kind, I reckoned the remainder of my life and found it more than the specified period, so I limited myself to half the provision and reserved the other half for myself." Solomon wondered at her great greed, and this is among the most wondrous guidance and gift. Among her greed is that she toils throughout the summer and gathers for winter, knowing that demand is scarce in winter and earning is difficult then, though she is weak yet very strong: she carries many times her own weight and drags it to her home.

Among the wonders of her condition: if you take a dried coriander seed and bring it near your nose, you will smell no scent from it. But when you place it on the ground, an ant comes to it from a distant place. If it cannot carry it, it goes and brings with it a line of ants to carry it. How did she perceive its scent from within her home so quickly and come to it? She perceives by smell from afar what others perceive by sight or hearing. She comes from a distant place to a spot where a person has eaten and some crumbs of bread or other remain, and she carries them off. If the item is larger than her, and she cannot carry it, she goes to her hole and brings with her a group of her companions, and they come like a black thread, one following another, until they help one another to lift and transport it. She comes to an ear of grain and smells it; if she finds it wheat, she cuts and tears it and carries it, but if she finds it barley, she does not. She has keen smell, lofty aspiration, great greed, and boldness in trying to move what is many times her weight. The ants have no leader or chief to direct them, as the bees have, except that they have a scout who seeks sustenance. When he finds it, he informs his companions, and they go out gathered together, each ant striving for the good of the group, not secretly taking any grain for herself apart from her companions.

Among the wonders of their condition: when a man wishes to protect himself from ants, so they do not fall into honey or the like, he digs a pit and places water around it, or takes a large vessel, fills it with water, and puts the thing in it. Then the ant that circles it cannot reach it; it climbs the wall and walks on the ceiling until it comes opposite the thing, and then throws itself upon it. We have tested this ourselves. Once a craftsman heated an iron ring in fire and threw it on the ground to cool, and it happened that an ant was enclosed in the ring. It moved in all directions to get out, but the heat of the fire overtook it, so it kept to the center and middle of the ring, which was its place, the farthest point from the rim.

[Section]

Then consider this weak ant and the cleverness Allah gave her in gathering food, storing it, preserving it, and warding off harm from it. You will see in that lessons and signs. You see that when a group of ants wants to secure food, they leave their trails seeking it. When they find it, they take a path from their trails to it and begin carrying it. You see two companies: one carrying what it has taken to their homes, going along, and another coming out of their homes toward it, not mixing with the first on the way, but like two threads, like a group of people going on a road and another group returning on the other side. When an item becomes too heavy for one, a group of ants gathers around it and helps carry it, like a log or stone that a group of people helps lift. If the one who found it is alone, her companions in the procession help her with it to her home and leave her and it. If the one who came upon it is a group, they help one another with it, then divide it at the door of the home.

Some knowledgeable people reported that he saw from them a wondrous thing one day. He said: "I saw an ant come to the half of a locust and try to lift it from the ground, but could not, so she went a short distance and came back with a group of ants. He said: 'So they lifted that half from the ground. When the ant with her company reached its place, they circled around it and searched, but found nothing, so they returned and put it down. Then she came back, found it, tried to lift it, could not, so she went a short distance and came back with them, lifted it, circled the place, and found nothing; so she went and put it down, then came back and brought them again, lifted it, and circled the place. When they found nothing, they formed a circle, placed that ant in the middle, then pressed upon her and cut her limb by limb, while I was watching.'"

Among the wonders of her intelligence is that when she carries grain to her homes, she breaks it, lest it sprout. If it is of the kind that the two halves sprout, she breaks it into four. When it is touched by dew and moisture and she fears decay, she brings it out to the sun and then returns it to her homes. This is why you sometimes see much grain at the doors of her homes, broken, and then soon after you do not see a single one of it.

And among her intelligence is that she does not make her settlement except on elevated ground, lest the flood overflow onto it and drown it. So you will never see an ant colony in the bottom of a valley, but at its top and above what the flood reaches.

Her intelligence is sufficiently shown by what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, stated in His Book about her words to the ant host when they saw Solomon, peace be upon him, and his hosts: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings; let not Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive.﴾

She spoke with ten kinds of address in this advice: calling, alerting, naming, commanding, stating, warning, specifying, informing, generalizing, and apologizing. Her counsel, with its brevity, included these ten types, and for this reason Solomon was amazed by her words, smiled laughing at them, and asked Allah to grant him the ability to thank Him for His blessing upon him when he heard her speech.

Do not consider such intelligence unlikely from a nation that glorifies its Lord, as is in the Sahih from the Prophet, who said:

A prophet of the prophets descended beneath a tree, and an ant bit him. So he ordered his belongings to be removed from under it, then he burned the ant colony. Then Allah revealed to him: "Because one ant bit you, you burned a nation of nations that glorify Me? Why not just one ant?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 27, verse 19:

The words of the Most High: ﴿My Lord, enable me (awzi'ni) to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that You approve of﴾

Ibn 'Abbas and the exegetes after him said: "Inspire me" (alhimni).

Abu Ishaq said: Its meaning in the language is "restrain me" (kuffani) from things, except for the very act of being grateful for Your favour. For this reason, the one who is "muwazza'" (zealously devoted) is explained as "muwalla'" (keenly attached to something).

From this comes the hadith:

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was muwazza' with regard to asking. That is, muwalla' with it, as if he were restrained and prevented from everything except it."

And in al-Sihah (Tahdhib of al-Jawhari's Sihah): "Wazza'tuhu azza'uhu wazan" means "I restrained him, so he restrained himself from it" (kaffa, i.e., he held back). "Awza'tuhu bi-al-shay'" means "I made him keen on the thing," so he became "muwza' bihi" (inclined to it). And "istawza'tu Allah shukrahu" means "I asked Allah to inspire me with His gratitude," so He inspired me (fa-awza'ni, i.e., astalhamtuhu fa-alhamani).

Thus the meaning of the word revolves around the sense of "inspire me to that, make me keen upon it, and restrain me from all else."

As for the Qadariyyah (Qadariyya, the early rationalist school denying divine predestination), they hold that this is not something decreed for the Lord, but rather something not decreed for the servant.

This hoopoe is among the most guided of creatures and the most perceptive of them regarding the places of water beneath the earth, which none other can see. Among his guidance is what Allah related of him in His Book, when he said to the Prophet of Allah, Sulayman, upon finding him missing and threatening him. When he came to him, he hastened to present his excuse before Sulayman could threaten him with punishment, and addressed him with words that stirred him to attend to what he said and to accept it from him. He said: ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge] of that which you have not encompassed﴾. Implicit in this is that "I have come to you with a matter I know thoroughly, such that I have comprehended it, and it is a great news of great importance." Therefore he said: ﴿And I have come to you from Sheba with certain news﴾.

Naba' (news) is information that carries importance, toward which souls are eager to attain knowledge. Then he described it as "certain news," with no doubt or uncertainty about it. This is an introduction before he informed the Prophet of Allah of that news, which emptied the listener's heart to receive the report and made him fully eager to hear and know it. This is a kind of opening eloquence (barā'at al-istihlāl) and an address that stirs excitement. Then he unveiled the reality of the report, unveiling it with emphatic proofs of affirmation, saying: "Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them." Then he informed about the state of that queen, that she was among the greatest of kings, in that she had been given of everything that kings may be given.

Then he increased the magnitude of her status by mentioning her throne upon which she sits, and that it is a mighty throne. Then he informed him of what calls them to be targeted and attacked in their own homeland, after inviting them to Allah, saying: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾.

The conjunction is omitted from this clause, and it is presented as independent, not coordinated with what precedes it, to indicate that it is the intended point, and what precedes it is a preparation for it. Then he informed about the one who misguides them and drives them to that, which is Satan's adorning their deeds for them, until he barred them from the straight path, which is prostration to Allah alone. Then he informed that this barrier stood between them and guidance and prostration to Allah, the only one worthy of prostration. Then he mentioned among the acts of Allah, glorified is He, the bringing forth of what is hidden (al-khabʾ) in the heavens and the earth, meaning what is concealed in them: rain, plants, minerals, and the kinds of what descends from the sky and what emerges from the earth. In the mention by the hoopoe of this matter, specifically among the acts of the Lord, the Exalted, there is an indication of what Allah singled him out with, namely bringing forth water hidden beneath the earth. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "In the bringing forth of what is hidden there is a sign that it is from the speech of the hoopoe, because of his expertise and his knowledge of water beneath the earth, and that is by inspiration from Him who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, may His power be exalted and His knowledge be subtle. What is hidden from one who has insight, looking by the light of Allah, are the signs of every person's craft or branch of knowledge in his appearance, speech, and character. No human performs an action except that Allah casts upon him the mantle of his action."

The real meaning of ʿistifa' (choosing, being selected): it is a form (iftiʿal) derived from tasfiyah (purification, clarifying), so that He has purified them from turbidities, and error is among the turbidities, so they are purified from it. This is not refuted by the case where they differ, because the truth has not passed them by, so the saying of one of them is not a turbidity; for opposing it would be a turbidity, and its clarification removes its being a turbidity. This is unlike the case where some of them say a statement that none of them opposes: if it were a false statement and no one rejected it, it would be the very essence of turbidity. This is because the disagreement of some of them with others is like following the Prophet (ﷺ) in some of his matters, which does not take them out of the essence of being chosen.

(Question)

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Is the peace from Allah, the Exalted, so that what is commanded is the praise, and the complete pause is upon it; or is it included in the speech and the command with both together?

The answer to this is that the statement admits both meanings, and each of them is supported by a kind of preponderance. It is preferred that it be included in the whole of the speech, for several reasons. Among them: its connection to it and its being conjoined to it without a separator; this requires that the verb "say" falls upon each of the two, and this is the original rule unless an obstacle prevents it. For this reason, when you say "Al-hamdu lillah wa subhan Allah," the glorification here is included in what is said. Among them: if it is conjoined to what is said, it is the conjoining of a declarative to a declarative, which is the original; and if it were cut off from it, it would be a conjoining to the imperative clause, and conjoining a declarative to an imperative is not good.

Among them: His saying ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ shows apparently that the one who gives the greeting is the one who says "All praise is for Allah," and for this reason the pronoun is in the third-person form and He did not say "peace upon My servants." What supports that the peace is from Allah, the Exalted, are several things. The first: its conformity to its counterparts in the Qur'an, such as His own peace upon His servants whom He has chosen, like His saying: "Peace upon Nuh among the worlds," "Peace upon Ibrahim," "Peace upon Musa and Harun," "Peace upon the family of Yasin."

Among them: His servants whom He has chosen are the messengers, and Allah, glorified is He, joins between His glorifying of Himself and His peace upon them, and between His praising of Himself and His peace upon them. As for the first, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers.﴾

He mentioned His declaring Himself free of what does not befit His majesty, and then His peace upon His messengers. In the joining of peace upon them with His glorifying of Himself there is a great secret of the secrets of the Qur'an, which contains a refutation of every falsifier and innovator: He declared Himself free of imperfection absolutely, just as He declared Himself free of what His creation says about Him, and then He gave peace to the messengers. This requires their safety from everything that those who deny them and oppose them say; and if they are safe from everything their enemies accused them of, it necessarily follows that everything they brought is safe from falsehood and corruption, and the greatest of what they brought is tawhid, the knowledge of Allah and describing Him with what befits His majesty, of what He described Himself with upon their tongues. When that is safe from lies, impossibility and corruption, it is pure truth, and whatever opposes it is falsehood, lies and impossibility. This very meaning is in His saying: ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾

For it includes His praise by what He has of attributes of perfection, qualities of majesty, praiseworthy acts and the Most Beautiful Names, and the safety of His messengers from every defect, imperfection and lie. That includes the safety of what they brought from every falsehood. So reflect upon this secret in the joining of peace upon His messengers with His praise and glorification. This supports that the peace here is from Allah, the Exalted, as it is at the end of al-Saffat.

As for conjoining a declarative to an imperative, how numerous it is. Among it is His saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth. Our Lord, the Most Merciful, the One sought for help against what you describe."﴾ And His saying: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ And His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of deciders.﴾ Its counterparts are very numerous.

The decisive word on this: it is said that the verse includes both matters together and unites them in one arrangement. The Messenger is the one who conveys from Allah His speech, and there is in it nothing but the conveying, and the speech is the speech of the Lord, blessed and exalted. He is the One who praised Himself and gave peace upon His servants, and He commanded His Messenger to convey that. So when the Messenger says "All praise is for Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen," he has praised Allah and given peace upon His servants with what He praised Himself with and gave peace with upon His servants. So it is peace from Allah in origin, from the one conveying it as a conveyance, and from the servants by way of following and obedience. So we say as our Lord, blessed and exalted, commanded us: ﴿All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen.﴾ A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Say: "He is Allah, the One."﴾ It is a declaration of tawhid from Him about Himself and a command to the addressee to affirm His oneness. So when the servant says ﴿Say: "He is Allah, the One."﴾ he has affirmed Allah with what He affirmed Himself with, and he brought the word "say" to realize this meaning, and that he is a pure conveyer, speaking what he was commanded to say. And Allah knows best.

This is unlike His saying: ﴿Say: "I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak."﴾ and ﴿Say: "I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind."﴾ For this is a pure command to originate the seeking of refuge, not a conveyance. And that is because Allah does not seek refuge from anyone, and that would be impossible for Him. This differs from His saying: ﴿Say: "He is Allah, the One."﴾ for it is a report about His oneness, and He, glorified is He, reports about Himself that He is the One, the Unique. So reflect upon this marvelous subtle point. And Allah is the One sought for help.

And he said in (Tariq al-Hijratayn):

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾

The word "al-salam" here may be included within the scope of the speech, so that it is conjoined to the declarative clause, "All praise is for Allah," and the command to speak embraces both clauses together. On this view, the pause falls on the last clause, and its position is accusative as reported speech after the verb of saying. It may also be a separate, independent resumed clause conjoined to the imperative clause; on this view it has no place in the grammatical analysis.

This estimate is the stronger, and on it the peace is from Allah upon them, which matches what preceded of His, glorified and exalted is He, peace upon His messengers, peace be upon them.

On the first estimate, it is a command to give peace upon them. But it may be said on this view: how is a declarative conjoined to an imperative when there is discord between them? It is not good to say: "Stand up and Zayd went," nor "Go out and sat, and ʿAmr." Or it may be answered that the imperative clause has been reported by a declarative clause, and despite this, conjoining a declarative to an imperative clause is not prohibited, since there is no discord or incongruity in the speech.

This is the parallel to His saying: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe."﴾ [Yunus: 101]. So His saying "But signs and warnings avail not" is not conjoined to the speech "Say," which is "look," but to the greater clause. Moreover, conjoining a declarative to an imperative is common, like His saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord, the Most Merciful, the One sought for help against what you describe."﴾ [al-Anbiya: 112]

And His saying: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 118]. The intent is that on this view Allah, the Exalted, has given peace upon the chosen among His servants, and the messengers are the best of them; and He, the Exalted, has informed that He purified them: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode. And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent.﴾ [Sad: 46-47]

It suffices for their excellence and nobility that Allah, the Exalted, singled them out with His revelation, made them trustees over His message and intermediaries between Him and His servants, and specified them with kinds of His honors: among them is one He took as a close friend, among them one with whom He spoke directly, and among them one whom He raised to a lofty station above the rest in degrees. He did not make for His servants access to Him except through them, nor entry into His Paradise except behind them, and He honored no one of them with a dignity except through their hands. So they are the nearest of creation to Him in means, the highest of them in rank with Him, and the dearest to Him and the most honored by Him.

In sum, the good of this world and the next is attained by the servants only through them, and through them Allah was known, through them He was worshipped and obeyed, and through them His beloved things were realized on earth.

[Chapter]

His saying, may He be exalted, in Surah al-Naml: ﴿Say: "Praise be to God, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen. Is God better, or what they associate with Him? Or who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down water for you from the sky, and with it We caused to grow gardens of delightful beauty, which you could never have caused their trees to grow? Is there a god besides God? Rather, they are a people who deviate."﴾ up to the end of the verses.

He argues against them that whoever alone did this for them is alone the God for them. If there were another lord who did this, then you should worship Him; and if there is no other lord who did this, then how do you set up another god alongside Him?

For this reason, the correct of the two opinions regarding the interpretation of the verse is: "Is there a god with God who did this?" Until the proof is complete, the answer must be "No." If there is no god with Him who does as He does, then how do you worship other gods besides Him? It is thereby known that the divinity of anything other than Him is false, just as the lordship of anything other than Him is false, by their own acknowledgment and your testimony.

As for the one who says: the meaning is "Is there another god with God?" without the meaning being "did this," his view is weak for two reasons:

The first: they used to say, "With God there are other gods," and they did not deny that.

The second: the proof is not complete, and their confounding and the establishment of the argument against them is not achieved except by this interpretation, namely: "If you say that He has no other god with Him, who did the like of His deed, then how do you set up with Him another god who creates nothing and is powerless?" This is like His saying: ﴿Or have they set up for God partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them? Say: God is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], and His saying: ﴿This is the creation of God; so show me what those besides Him have created.﴾ [Luqman: 11], and His saying: ﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], and His saying: ﴿And those they invoke besides God create nothing, while they are themselves created.﴾ [al-Nahl: 20], and His saying: ﴿And they have taken besides Him gods who create nothing, while they are themselves created.﴾ [al-Furqan: 3]. This is abundant in the Qur'an, and by it the argument is completed, as has been made clear.

The point is that the servant attains this in the witnessing that comes from contemplating the offenses and sins, and their running upon him and upon creation by the decree of the Mighty, the Wise; and that there is no protector from His wrath and the causes of His displeasure except Him; and there is no path to obeying Him except with His help; and no arrival at His good pleasure except by His enabling. So the sources of all affairs are from Him, their return is to Him, and the reins of enabling are all in His hands. There is no seeking of help for the servants except from Him, and no reliance except upon Him, as Shu'ayb, the orator of the prophets, said: ﴿And my enabling is only by God; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn in repentance.﴾ [Hud: 88].

((Part Twelve))

[Section: Supplication is among the most beneficial remedies]

Supplication (du'a') is among the most beneficial remedies. It is the enemy of affliction (bala'): it repels it, treats it, prevents its descent, lifts it, or lightens it once it has descended. It is the weapon of the believer.

As al-Hakim narrated in his Sahih, from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is the weapon of the believer, the pillar of the religion, and the light of the heavens and the earth."

For supplication in the face of affliction there are degrees.

It has three states in relation to affliction:

The first: that it is stronger than the affliction, so it repels it.

The second: that it is weaker than the affliction, so the affliction prevails over it and the servant is struck by it, but supplication may still lighten it, even if it is weak.

The third: that the two are equal, and each one prevents the other.

Al-Hakim also narrated in his Sahih, from the hadith of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Caution does not avail against decree. Supplication benefits with regard to what has descended and what has not descended. Indeed, affliction descends, and supplication meets it, and the two wrestle with each other until the Day of Resurrection."

Also in it, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Supplication benefits with regard to what has descended and what has not descended, so upon you, servants of Allah, is supplication."

Also in it, from the hadith of Thawban, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Nothing turns back the decree except supplication, and nothing increases the lifespan except righteousness, and a man is deprived of provision because of a sin he commits."

[Section: Persistence in supplication]

Among the most beneficial remedies is persistence (ilah') in supplication.

Ibn Majah narrated in his Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, He will be angry with him."

In the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not be weak in supplication, for no one perishes while supplicating."

Al-Awza'i mentioned, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah loves those who are persistent (al-mulihhin) in supplication."

In the Kitab al-Zuhd of Imam Ahmad, from Qatadah, who said: Muwarriq said: "I have found no likeness for the believer except a man on a plank in the sea, who calls: 'O Lord, O Lord,' hoping that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will rescue him."

[Section: Among the afflictions of supplication]

Among the hindrances that prevent the effect of supplication from following it is that the servant becomes hasty, finds the answer slow, becomes weary (yastahsir), and abandons supplication. He is like one who sows a seed or plants a sapling, then tends it and waters it, but when he is slow to see its completion and maturity, he leaves it and neglects it.

In al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of you will be answered so long as he does not hasten, saying: 'I supplicated, but I was not answered.'"

In the Sahih of Muslim, from him: "The servant will continue to be answered so long as he does not supplicate for sin or the severing of ties of kinship, and so long as he does not hasten." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is hastening?" He said: "He says, 'I have supplicated, and I have supplicated, and I have not seen that I am answered,' and then he becomes weary and abandons supplication."

In the Musnad of Ahmad, from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The servant will remain in good so long as he does not hasten." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how does one hasten?" He said: "He says, 'I have supplicated my Lord, but He has not answered me.'"

[Section: Times of answer]

When one combines with supplication the presence of the heart and its complete concentration upon the object sought, and it coincides with one of the six times of answer, which are:

The last third of the night; at the time of the adhan; between the adhan and the iqamah; after the obligatory prayers; when the imam ascends the pulpit on Friday until the prayer of that day is concluded; and the last hour after 'Asr.

And it coincides with humility in the heart, brokenness before the Lord, submission to Him, supplication, and tenderness.

The supplicant faces the qiblah.

He is in a state of purity (ta'harah).

He raises his hands to Allah.

He begins with praise of Allah and extolling Him.

Then he follows with blessing upon Muhammad, His servant and Messenger (ﷺ).

Then he precedes his need with repentance and seeking forgiveness.

Then he enters upon Allah, persists before Him in asking, implores Him with humility, and calls upon Him with desire and fear.

He seeks a means to Him through His names, attributes, and His oneness.

He offers charity before his supplication, for this supplication is hardly ever rejected, especially if it coincides with the supplications which the Prophet (ﷺ) informed were most likely to be answered, or which contain the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam).

[Transmitted supplications]

Among them is what is in the Sunan (and in) the Sahih of Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "heard a man saying: 'O Allah, I ask You, by virtue of my testifying that You are Allah, there is no god but You, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is begotten, and to whom no one is equal.' He said: 'He has asked Allah by the Name by which, when He is asked, He gives, and when He is called upon, He answers.'" And in another wording: "You have asked Allah by His Greatest Name."

In the Sunan and the Sahih of Ibn Hibban also, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik: "He was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when a man was praying, then he supplicated: 'O Allah, I ask You, by virtue of Yours is all praise, there is no god but You, the Bestower, Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor, O Living, O Self-Subsisting.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'He has supplicated Allah by His Great Name, which when He is called upon by it, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives.'"

Ahmad recorded both hadiths in his Musnad.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in these two verses: ﴿And your God is One God; there is no god except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], and the opening of Al 'Imran: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah — there is no god except Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan sahih hadith.

In the Musnad of Ahmad and the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadiths of Abu Hurayrah, Anas ibn Malik, and Rabi'ah ibn 'Amir, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Persist with 'Ya Dhal-Jalali wal-Ikram' (O Possessor of Majesty and Honor)" — meaning: cling to it, keep to it, and be constant in it.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "When a matter worried the Prophet (ﷺ), he would raise his head to the sky, and when he strove in supplication he would say: 'Ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum.'"

Also in it, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: "When a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would say: 'Ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum, bi-rahmatika astaghith' (O Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek relief)."

In the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in three suras of the Qur'an: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, and Ta-Ha." Al-Qasim said: "So I searched for it, and it was the verse ﴿Al-Hayyu al-Qayyum﴾."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi and the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The supplication of Dhu'l-Nun, when he called while in the belly of the whale: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. No Muslim supplicates with it for anything except that Allah answers him." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sahih hadith.

In the Mustadrak of al-Hakim also, from the hadith of Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not inform you of something which, if a serious matter befalls one of you, and he supplicates with it, Allah will relieve him of it? It is the supplication of Dhu'l-Nun."

Also in his Sahih, from him, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Shall I direct you to the Greatest Name of Allah? It is the supplication of Yunus." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, was it only for Yunus?" He said: "Do you not hear His saying: ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 88]? Any Muslim who supplicates with it during his illness forty times, and then dies during that illness, will be given the reward of a martyr, and if he recovers, he recovers forgiven."

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say at times of distress: "There is no god but Allah, the Great, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the seven heavens, Lord of the earth, and Lord of the Noble Throne."

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught me that when distress befalls me I should say: 'There is no god but Allah, the Forbearing, the Generous. Glory be to Allah, and blessed is Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"

In his Musnad also, from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No worry or grief ever befalls anyone who says: 'O Allah, I am Your servant, son of Your servant, son of Your maidservant; my forelock is in Your hand; Your judgment over me is binding; Your decree concerning me is just. I ask You, O Allah, by every name which is Yours, by which You named Yourself, or which You taught to any of Your creation, or which You revealed in Your Book, or which You kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You, that You make the Great Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my breast, the dispeller of my grief, and the departure of my worry,' except that Allah removes his worry and grief and replaces them with joy." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not learn it?" He said: "Yes, whoever hears it should learn it."

Ibn Mas'ud also said: "No prophet of the prophets was ever distressed except that he sought relief through glorification (tasbih)."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned in the Kitab al-Mujabin and in al-Du'a', from al-Hasan, who said: There was a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the Ansar, known as Abu Mu'allaq, who was a merchant trading with his own wealth and that of others, travelling far and wide. He was devout and scrupulous. Once he set out, and a masked robber armed with weapons met him and said: "Put down what you have, for I will kill you." He said: "What do you want of my blood? Take the wealth." He said: "As for the wealth, it is mine; I want only your blood." He said: "Since you refuse, then let me pray four rak'ahs." He said: "Pray as you wish." So he performed ablution and prayed four rak'ahs, and among his supplications in the last prostration was: "O Loving, O Loving, O Lord of the Glorious Throne, O Doer of what You will, I ask You by Your might which cannot be overcome, and by Your dominion which cannot be wronged, and by Your light which fills the pillars of Your Throne, that You suffice me against the evil of this robber. O Helper, help me," three times. Then behold, a horseman came toward him with a spear held between the ears of his horse. When the robber saw him, he advanced toward him, and the horseman stabbed him and killed him. Then he came to him and said: "Arise." He said: "Who are you, may my father and mother be your ransom? Allah has relieved me through you today." He said: "I am an angel from the people of the fourth heaven. When you supplicated with your first supplication, I heard a rattling at the gates of heaven. Then when you supplicated with your second, I heard a clamor among the people of heaven. Then when you supplicated with your third, it was said to me: 'The supplication of one in distress,' so I asked Allah to let me be the one to kill him."

Al-Hasan said: Whoever performs ablution, prays four rak'ahs, and supplicates with this supplication, will be answered, whether he is distressed or not.

[Section: Circumstances of supplication]

Often you find supplications by which people supplicated and were answered, but accompanying the supplication was the necessity of its speaker and his turning to Allah, or a good deed that preceded from him, which Allah, glorified is He, made the answer to his call a thanks for his good deed, or it coincided with a time of answer, and similar things, so his supplication was answered. Then the observer supposes that the secret lies in the wording of that supplication, and takes it in isolation from those circumstances which accompanied it from that supplicant. This is like when a man uses a beneficial medicine at the right time and in the right manner, and benefits from it, and another supposes that using this medicine by itself suffices to attain the desired result; he would be mistaken. This is a point in which many people err.

From this also: one may supplicate at a grave out of necessity and be answered, and the ignorant person supposes the secret lies in the grave, while he does not know that the secret lies in necessity and sincere turning to Allah. When this occurs in one of the houses of Allah, it is better and more beloved to Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 27, verse 65:**

Reflect on how the heavens are mentioned in plural form in His words: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾. Since the intended meaning is to negate knowledge of the unseen from everyone who is in any one of the heavens, He mentioned them in the plural.

**(Section)**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception where the excluded item is not of the same category as what precedes it), and it came in the dialect of the Tamim tribe. Although it is correct to say that Allah is in the heavens and the earth, that is only figurative, because He is exalted above being located in a place. This differs from others, for saying of them that they are in the heaven or on the earth is not figurative but literal. It is not valid to apply one expression in one situation to both the literal and the figurative sense."

I say: His statement "in the dialect of the Tamim" means that among their usages is that a disjunctive exception may be treated like a connected one (istithna' muttasil) if the exception is valid with the excluded item. This is valid here, since it is correct to say: None knows the unseen except Allah.

Ibn Malik said: "In my view, the correct position is that the exception in the verse is connected (muttasil), and (fi, 'in') is related to a verb other than istaqarra (to be settled/fixed) from the verbs that are attributed literally both to Allah, exalted is He, and to created beings, such as dhakara (to mention) and yudhkaru (is mentioned) and the like, as if it were said: None in the heavens and the earth who is mentioned knows the unseen except Allah, exalted is He."

He said: "It is also permissible to relate (fi) to istaqarra, with the verb attached to a omitted noun (mudaf) and the noun it was attached to put in its place. The original would be: None whose mention is established in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah. Then the verb and the mudaf were omitted, and the pronoun became hidden because it is in the nominative case. This applies on the assumption that the literal and figurative senses cannot both be intended in one situation, though in my view this is not impossible, based on their sayings: the pen is one of the two tongues, and the maternal uncle is one of the two parents."

And His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ (33:56).

And His words (ﷺ): "The hands are three: the hand of Allah, the hand of the giver, and the hand of the receiver." End of his words.

This, then, is the statement of these two distinguished scholars on this verse.

You see the obvious artificiality in it, which the verse does not need. Rather, the matter in the verse is clearer than that. The correct view regarding the exception in this verse is that it is connected, and there is no use of one expression in both its literal and figurative senses in the verse. This is because "those in the heavens and the earth" here is among the most emphatic forms of generality, and it does not refer to a specific individual. It is therefore equivalent in force to "anyone," as in your saying: None knows the unseen except Allah. The mention of the heavens and the earth is included to affirm the intention of generality and comprehensiveness. So the sentence conveys the meaning of "no one knows the unseen except Allah." The confusion arose from their assumption that the adverbial phrase here serves to restrict and specify, but that is not so. It serves rather to confirm total inclusiveness and comprehensiveness. It is like the description in His words: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ (6:38). That description does not restrict but confirms the flying implied by "bird." Likewise His words ﴿those in the heavens and the earth﴾ confirm the comprehensiveness that the negation intends. Whoever reflects on the verse will know that this is the only thing it intends.

It has also been said that there is no impediment to describing Allah, exalted is He, as being in the heavens, just as He described Himself and as His Messenger described Him. They said: It does not follow that this description is figurative. Rather, He has a reality of it that befits His majesty, and nothing of His creation shares in it. This is like describing Him as Hearing, Seeing, Knowing, Powerful, Living, and Willing in the literal sense, while these same attributes are also applied to His creation in the literal sense. The reality specific to Him does not resemble the reality of His creation. Thus applying the attribute literally to both does not necessitate their resemblance, so there is no need to flee to figurative interpretation.

As for his statement that the adverbial phrase is related to a verb other than istaqarra, such as dhakara and yudhkaru, which are attributed literally to Allah and to created beings, and so on: it is said that the omission of the operator of an adverbial phrase is permissible only when it is a general "being" or a general "settling." When it is a specific, restricted settling or being, its omission is not permitted. This is confirmed in His words: ﴿when he saw it settled before him﴾ (27:40), because what is meant is the settling that means firmness and permanence, not mere presence before him. How then can the omission of the operator of the adverbial phrase be justified in a position where such omission is not customary? Even further from this is the second supposition he mentioned, that the operator of the adverbial phrase is a settling attached to a mention that has been omitted, the noun being dispensed with in place of the attached noun, the sense being "its mention is settled." This has no parallel, and it is an omission with no evidence for it. A noun may be dispensed with in place of its attached noun only under two conditions: that it be expressed, and that its meaning be known and indicated, to avoid ambiguity.

As for the claim that something omitted is attached to something omitted, and then the attached noun is attached to yet another omitted thing without any indication in the wording, this is something eloquent speech is protected from, let alone the speech of the Lord of the worlds.

As for his claim that it is not impossible to intend the literal and the figurative sense together, and his proof by their saying "the pen is one of the two tongues": there is no need for it, because "two tongues" is a dual form, standing in place of two named things, one of which is meant literally and the other figuratively. Likewise "the maternal uncle is one of the two parents," and likewise "the hands are three."

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾, the argument from it is even further off than all of this. The blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) from Allah and from His angels are literal beyond doubt. The literal sense attributed to Allah from this does not resemble the literal sense attributed to the angels. Just as when it is said: Allah and His Messenger and the believers know that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, it is not permissible to say that this is using a single expression in both its literal and figurative senses, even though the knowledge attributed to Allah is not identical to the knowledge attributed to His Messenger and the believers. So reflect on these subtle points. Praise and grace belong to Allah.

(Section heading)

As for "God hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), al-Suhayli said: the object of "sami'a" is omitted, because hearing is connected to speech and sounds and not to other things. So the lam (li-) keeps its own function, except that it indicates an additional meaning, namely responding (al-istijabah) that accompanies hearing. Thus the word combines brevity with indication of the additional meaning, which is the response to the one who praises Him. This is like His words ﴿Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten has drawn close to you﴾. The lam here is not the lam of the object, as they claim, nor is it extra. Rather, "radifa" (ridf) is a transitive verb whose complement is other than this noun, just as the object of "sami'a" is other than the prepositional phrase.

The meaning of "radifa" is "to follow, to come after, to come in the wake of." If you consider it carefully, applying it to the noun governed by the lam would give an incorrect meaning. Rather, the meaning is: "there has followed you your urgency and your saying," because they said, "When is this promise?"

Then the object, which is the saying and the urgency, is omitted, relying on the listener's understanding.

The lam indicates the omission, because it prevents the noun it governs from being the object, and it also indicates another benefit, namely the meaning of "ajjala lakum" (hastened for you), so it is connected to that meaning. Thus the sense of the statement becomes: "Say: perhaps there has hastened for you some of what you are seeking to hasten, so there followed your saying and your seeking of haste for you."

So "radifa" indicates that they said and sought haste, and the lam indicates the other meaning, and the statement is arranged in the best order, combining brevity with completeness of meaning.

Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 27, verse 79:

He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to rely upon Him (tawakkul), and he followed this command with that which necessitates tawakkul, validates it, and calls for its establishment and realisation, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth﴾. For the servant's being upon the truth necessitates the realisation of the station of tawakkul upon Allah, sufficing oneself with Him, and taking refuge in His firm pillar. Indeed, Allah is the Truth, the Protector of the Truth, its Helper and its Supporter, and the Sufficient for whoever stands for Him, sincerely for the Truth. So how could one who is upon the truth not rely upon Him?

And how could he fear while he is upon the truth?

As the Messengers said to their peoples: ﴿And why should we not rely upon Allah, when He has guided us to our paths?﴾ [Ibrahim: 12]

So they marvelled at their (the peoples') abandonment of reliance upon Allah when He had guided them, and they acknowledged that this would never be the case.

It may be said: the negation of making the deaf hear, together with the negation of making the dead hear, indicates that what is meant is the incapacity of each of them to hear, and that since the hearts of these people were dead and deaf, making them hear was impossible, being like addressing the dead and the deaf.

This is true. However, the negation does not exclude the hearing of the souls after death, hearing of reproach and rebuke, through their connection with the bodies at some time. This is other than the negated hearing. And Allah knows best.

The real meaning is: you cannot make hear the one whom Allah has not willed to make hear. ﴿You are only a warner﴾, that is, Allah has only given you the ability to warn, which He has charged you with, not the ability to make hear those whom Allah has not willed to make hear.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 27, verse 88:

As for the word al-Sani' (the Maker, the Fashioner), it has not come in the names of the Lord, glory be to Him, and it is not possible for it to be among them. The sani' is one who makes something, whether it is just or unjust, foolish or wise, permissible or impermissible. And whatever name's meaning is divided between praise and blame is not found as an absolute name among the Most Beautiful Names, such as al-Fa'il (the Doer), al-'Amil (the Worker), al-Sani' (the Maker), al-Murid (the Willer) and al-Mutakallim (the Speaker), because the meanings of these names are divided into the praiseworthy and the blameworthy. This is unlike al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), al-Qadir (the All-Powerful), al-Hayy (the Ever-Living), al-Sami' (the All-Hearing) and al-Basir (the All-Seeing). And the Prophet (ﷺ) has named the servant a sani'.

Al-Bukhari said: Ali ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, Marwan ibn Mu'awiya narrated to us, Abu Malik narrated to us, from Rib'i ibn Khirash, from Hudhayfa, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah fashions every maker and his making."

And He, glory be to Him, has applied the name al-Sun' (the making, the workmanship) to His own act, saying: ﴿The handiwork of Allah, who has perfected all things﴾. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them rigid, while they pass away as the passing of clouds﴾ indicates the workmanship.

It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an object, meaning: "Look at the handiwork of Allah." According to the first view, ṣun' Allah is a verbal noun in the sense of the act; according to the second, it is in the sense of the thing made (al-maṣnu', the object made), since that is what can be looked at and seen.
